The variable aperture lens on the new iPhone 18 Pro is nearly a full stop wider than the fixed aperture lens on the previous generation: jumping from f/1.78 on the iPhone 17 Pro to f/1.48 (the smaller the number, the larger the aperture).

In theory, this should result in a more pronounced shallow depth-of-field effect, creating stronger separation between subject and background — but the difference is actually quite subtle. There are in fact four ways to achieve a shallow depth-of-field effect using iPhones from many generations back……

Portrait Mode

The most obvious method is, of course, Portrait mode, which is designed precisely to clearly separate a person from the background.

This works entirely through computational photography (aided by LiDAR on models equipped with it) to identify the subject, then artificially applies blur to the rest. The first-generation version produced very rough results, but in recent years it has become quite impressive.

Macro Photography

The second method is Macro mode, which automatically activates when you get very close to your subject. Once enabled, the iPhone will switch to the ultra-wide lens, which is capable of focusing at extremely close distances.

When using this mode, only a few centimetres will remain in focus, with everything further away becoming increasingly blurred. As you can see in the example below, before shooting with this mode, be prepared to spend a lot of time wiping away dust and cleaning up! When you see the yellow flower icon appear in the bottom-right corner of the screen, it indicates that Macro mode is active.

Getting Close to the Subject

You can also use the standard lens and get very close to your subject to achieve a similar effect. For example:

Before taking the photo, simply tap on the object or person you want to focus on.

Telephoto Lens

The final factor affecting depth of field is focal length. All else being equal, the longer the focal length, the shallower the depth of field, so using the iPhone's telephoto lens can also produce a certain degree of background blur.

Combining All Three Methods

Combining all three methods yields the best results:

  • Use the telephoto lens
  • Keep the subject as far from the background as possible
  • Get as close to the subject as possible

When shooting portraits, this is the ideal approach, and it works particularly well on the iPhone 15 Pro and later models, as these are equipped with longer focal lengths.

Conclusion

The wider variable aperture lens is just one of many new camera features on the iPhone 18 Pro, and if photography is important to you, the upgrade is worth it. But if your goal is simply background blur, there are in fact other ways to achieve the same effect.
